title: Five independent days versus five copies of one random day
scenario_markdown: Daily demand has mean 20 units and variance 9 units squared. Define S=X1+...+X5 for five independent, identically distributed days, and T=5X for five times one random day's demand. These are different random quantities despite having the same expected value.
assumptions: The five Xi in S are independent and have identical finite moments.
T repeats the same random X five times, not independent draws.

stages.prompt_markdown: What is Var(S) in squared demand units? Select the value rounded to four decimal places.

options.hint_markdown: Independent days have zero covariance; add five daily variances.
Variance is given as 9; do not replace it with SD=3 before summing variances.

stages.explanation_markdown: $\operatorname{Var}(S)=5(9)=45$. SD is $\sqrt{45}$, whereas the expected sum is 5(20)=100. Excel variance arithmetic: `=5*9`.

stages.prompt_markdown: What is Var(T) in squared demand units? Select the value rounded to four decimal places.

options.hint_markdown: Scaling one random variable squares the multiplier.
The variance scaling rule uses 5 squared, not 5 times the SD.

stages.prompt_markdown: Why do these variances differ even though E[S]=E[T]=100?

options.text_markdown: S combines independent draws; T repeats the identical draw, so all five components move together.
Linearity of expectation fails for T.
options.hint_markdown: Expectation is linear with or without independence.

options.text_markdown: Equal means mathematically require equal variances.
options.hint_markdown: Location and dispersion are different distribution features.

stages.explanation_markdown: Independence removes cross-covariances in S. In T, each copy is perfectly dependent on the others. The distinction is probabilistic structure, not merely algebraic appearance.
